sections.Introduction:
The ribs form the bony framework of the thoracic cavity (see Image. Thoracic Cage). The thoracic cage generally contains 12 pairs of ribs. Each rib articulates posteriorly with 2 thoracic vertebrae at the costovertebral joints. The first rib is an exception because it articulates only with the first thoracic vertebra.

[Figure] Thoracic Cage. This diagram illustrates the skeletal structure of the human thoracic cage and its primary anatomical components. A full-body skeletal outline on the left provides overall regional context, while the magnified 3-dimensional model on the right highlights the structural relationship between the bony ribs and the central sternum. Segmented blue shading clearly distinguishes the flexible costal cartilage from the rigid osseous components. Contributed by Bruno Bordoni, PhD

The ribs are classified as true, false, or floating according to their sternal attachment. The first 7 ribs are true ribs and articulate directly with the sternum through their costal cartilages. The 8th, 9th, and 10th ribs are false ribs and articulate indirectly with the sternum because their costal cartilages join the 7th costal cartilage at the costochondral joints. Floating ribs are traditionally defined as ribs that lack sternal articulation and classically include the 11th and 12th ribs. However, the 10th rib frequently lacks attachment to the ninth rib and may also be classified as a floating rib.[1] True ribs articulate with the sternum at the sternocostal joints. The first sternocostal joint is an exception because it is a synarthrosis. The first rib may also articulate with the clavicle at the costoclavicular joint.[2]

Results from recent cadaveric studies demonstrated substantial variability in costal margin anatomy compared with traditional descriptions. Results from a 2023 study of 30 cadavers showed that the 10th rib lacked attachment to the ninth rib and was a floating rib in more than 50% of specimens. Results from the same study showed direct attachment of the eighth rib to the sternum without joining the seventh rib in 10% of cadavers. Results from another study of 40 cadavers found a floating 10th rib in 59% of specimens and mobility of the ninth rib tip in 86% of evaluations.[3]
sections.Structure and Function:
The ribs typically have the following anatomical components (see Image. Posterior View of a Typical Rib):

Most ribs are typical, possessing all of these features. Atypical ribs that lack some of these characteristics include the 1st, 2nd, 10th, 11th, and 12th ribs. The first rib is atypical because it is short and wide and has 2 costal grooves and a single articular facet. The 2nd rib is thin and long and has a tuberosity on its superior surface for attachment of the serratus anterior muscle (see Image. Superior View of the Second Rib). The 10th rib has only 1 articular facet. The 11th and 12th ribs each have a single articular facet and lack a neck.

[Figure] Superior View of the Second Rib. This anatomical illustration displays the superior surface of the human 2nd rib, highlighting its unique muscular insertion landmarks. A prominent roughened tuberosity near the center features labeled attachment sites for the 1st and 2nd digitations of the serratus anterior muscle. The posterior aspect indicates the distinct structural angle of the bone, distinguishing its atypical morphology from typical lower thoracic ribs. Henry Vandyke Carter, Public Domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Results from a 2024 cadaveric study found that the 10th rib was floating in 46% of specimens and that the 8th and 9th ribs had free tips in 58% and 92% of evaluations, respectively. Bridging interchondral joints occurred most commonly between the fifth and eighth ribs and participated in distributing forces from the costal margin across the chest wall. Upward forces at the costal margin were transmitted across the lower rib cage, resulting in increased mobility of the lower ribs.[4]
sections.Blood Supply and Lymphatics:
The ribs receive blood supply anteriorly from the anterior intercostal arteries and posteriorly from the posterior intercostal arteries. The anterior intercostal arteries of the first to the seventh ribs branch from the internal thoracic artery. In contrast, the anterior intercostal arteries of the 8th to 10th ribs derive from the musculophrenic artery.

The posterior intercostal arteries supply the 1st to 10th ribs posteriorly. The first and second posterior intercostal arteries arise from the superior intercostal artery, a branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery. The remaining posterior intercostal arteries derive from the descending thoracic aorta.

Floating ribs differ in vascular supply because of their short length and lack of sternal articulation and receive arterial blood only from posterior vessels. The 11th rib receives blood supply from the 11th posterior intercostal artery, whereas the subcostal artery perfuses the 12th rib. Corresponding venous drainage follows a similar segmental arrangement.

The costal veins follow the same nomenclature as the arteries but differ in their drainage patterns. The anterior intercostal veins drain into the internal thoracic and musculophrenic veins. The posterior intercostal veins empty into the azygos and hemiazygos systems. The subcostal vein drains the 12th rib.

All intercostal arteries and veins course within the costal groove of their corresponding ribs. However, the intercostal artery is not consistently protected within the costal groove. Results from a computed tomography–based study of 298 arteries demonstrated that the intercostal artery is exposed within the intercostal space during the first 6 cm lateral to the spine. At a distance of 3 cm from the spine, only 17% of arteries were shielded by the superior rib, compared with 97% at 6 cm. Results also showed significantly greater variability in arterial position among older patients and within more cephalad intercostal spaces.[10] These findings have important implications for safe chest tube insertion and thoracentesis because they challenge the traditional concept that the neurovascular bundle is consistently protected within the subcostal groove.[11]
sections.Nerves:
The intercostal nerves supply the ribs through sensory and motor branches. These nerves course between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and lie inferior to the blood vessels within the costal groove. Branches arise after the nerves exit the costal groove. The lateral cutaneous branches innervate the skin of the lateral thoracic wall. These branches pierce the external intercostal muscle and divide into anterior and posterior branches. The anterior cutaneous branches provide sensory innervation to the skin of the anterior thorax and reach the skin near the midline. The pleural sensory branches innervate the parietal pleura. The peritoneal sensory branches course within the parietal peritoneum and arise from the 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, and 11th intercostal nerves. The collateral branch courses along the superior border of the rib immediately inferior to its corresponding intercostal nerve. The muscular branches innervate the intercostal muscles. The rami communicantes connect the intercostal nerves to the sympathetic ganglia.

Results from recent cadaveric studies demonstrated substantial variability in the branching anatomy and course of the intercostal nerves at the costal margin. Results from a 2025 study showed that the seventh, eighth, and ninth intercostal nerves each give rise to a diaphragmatic branch and arborize at the costochondral junction, providing branches to the diaphragm and abdominal wall musculature, with additional arborization at the lower rib tips. The location of the seventh and eighth intercostal nerves varied according to the associated costal margin anatomy, particularly depending on whether the eighth rib attached directly to the sternum, which occurred in 42% of specimens, or joined the seventh rib to form the costal margin, which occurred in 58% of specimens.[12] This anatomic variability has important implications for procedures involving the costal margin, including intercostal nerve blocks and chest wall surgical procedures.
sections.Muscles:
Many muscles act on the ribs and influence rib movement. The anatomy and functions of these muscles are described below. The pectoralis major has clavicular and sternocostal heads. The clavicular head originates from the anterior surface of the medial half of the clavicle, whereas the sternocostal head arises from the anterior surface of the sternum, the proximal 6 costal cartilages, and the external abdominal oblique aponeurosis. The muscle inserts on the lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. The medial pectoral nerve innervates the sternocostal head, and the lateral pectoral nerve innervates the clavicular head. The pectoralis major functions as an accessory muscle of inspiration.

The pectoralis minor originates from the third, fourth, and fifth ribs and inserts on the coracoid process of the scapula. This muscle lies deep to the pectoralis major and receives innervation from the medial pectoral nerve. Contraction of the pectoralis minor elevates the ribs when the scapula is fixed. The muscle also functions as an accessory muscle of inspiration.

The external abdominal oblique originates from the 5th through 12th ribs and inserts on the xiphoid process, pubic crest, outer lip of the iliac crest, linea alba, pubic tubercle, anterior superior iliac spine, and inguinal ligament. Contraction of this muscle depresses the ribs and compresses the abdominal cavity, thereby increasing intra-abdominal pressure. Innervation arises from the anterior branches of the lower 6 thoracoabdominal nerves and the subcostal nerve on each side.

The rectus abdominis originates from the pubic crest and inserts on the fifth, sixth, and seventh costal cartilages and the xiphoid process. Innervation derives from the thoracoabdominal and subcostal nerves. Contraction draws the rib cage and pelvis inward toward the abdomen and assists with active expiration.

The subclavius originates from the first rib and its costal cartilage and inserts on the subclavian groove of the clavicle. The nerve to the subclavius provides innervation. Contraction of the subclavius elevates the first rib.
sections.Physiologic Variants:
The rib cage volume is approximately 10% smaller in women than in men. Nevertheless, the craniocaudal inclination of the ribs is greater in women. The ribs also tend to grow longer relative to the axial skeleton in women than in men.[19]

Results from 3D geometric morphometric studies demonstrated that sex-specific trajectories of thoracic size and shape diverge at approximately 12 years of age and continue to diverge slightly with aging. Adult male rib cages are deeper, shorter, and wider than female rib cages and have more horizontally oriented ribs. These differences likely reflect pubertal changes in body composition and differences in reproductive anatomy.[20]

Functionally, rib cage muscles contribute more to resting inspiration in women because of greater rib inclination. In contrast, a wider lower rib cage in men is associated with a greater diaphragmatic contribution to breathing kinematics.[21][22] Thoracic shape depends on both age and sex. Adolescent anterior thoracic growth occurs in 3 distinct phases: an initial slow increase in volume, a stabilization phase, and a subsequent period of more rapid growth.[23]

Normal rib variants include cervical, intrathoracic, and pelvic ribs; forked, or bifid, ribs; rib fusion and bridging; and pseudarthrosis of the first rib. Numerical and structural rib abnormalities occur in approximately 0.15% to 3.4% of individuals. Supernumerary ribs, including cervical and lumbar ribs, account for approximately 30% of all congenital costal anomalies. Missing ribs account for 26% of these anomalies, whereas segmentation defects and synostoses occur in 20%.[24] Results from a comprehensive 2023 review of pediatric rib abnormalities classified rib lesions as focal, multifocal, or diffuse and emphasized a pattern-recognition approach to radiographic interpretation.[25]
sections.Surgical Considerations:
The ribs have important clinical relationships with the underlying thoracic structures. Knowledge of these relationships is essential for the safe performance of thoracic procedures. Rib counting by palpation helps determine appropriate sites for thoracentesis and tube thoracostomy. Additionally, rib counting guides selection of the appropriate surgical entry site for thoracic procedures.

Surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF) has received increasing attention during the past decade. The 2025 World Society of Emergency Surgery–American Association for the Surgery of Trauma Thoracic Trauma Guidelines recommend consideration of SSRF in all hemodynamically stable patients with flail chest and performance of the procedure within 48 to 72 hours after injury. Consideration of SSRF is also recommended for patients with 3 or more ipsilateral, severely displaced rib fractures involving the 3rd through 10th ribs and an inadequate response to mechanical ventilation or inability to wean from ventilatory support.[26]

Results from a 2025 nationwide analysis of the American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Improvement Program from 2017 through 2021 demonstrated that SSRF was associated with lower mortality than nonoperative treatment, at 1.5% compared with 2.7%. The mortality benefit was most pronounced in patients with flail chest, at 4.2% compared with 10.1%. Early SSRF within 82 hours was associated with lower rates of acute respiratory distress syndrome and ventilator-associated pneumonia.[27]

However, results from the 2026 multicenter Surgery of Fractured Ribs randomized controlled trial showed that routine SSRF did not reduce intensive care unit length of stay and was associated with longer hospitalization and higher pneumonia rates. Results from the trial also demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements in quality of life and pain outcomes, supporting selective rather than routine use of SSRF.[28]

Hemodynamic instability is an absolute contraindication to SSRF. Traumatic brain injury and pulmonary contusion are no longer considered absolute contraindications and warrant individualized evaluation. Advanced age, significant cardiopulmonary comorbidities, and active malignant neoplasms are relative contraindications that also require individualized assessment.[29]
sections.Clinical Significance:
Rib fractures are common and account for approximately 12% of all fractures.[31] The risk increases with age. Other common rib abnormalities include rib dislocation, costochondritis, and osteoporosis.[32][33] Slipping rib syndrome is an increasingly recognized but still underdiagnosed condition caused by abnormal mobility of the 8th through 10th ribs. Diagnosis is primarily clinical and may be confirmed with the hooking maneuver and supplemented by dynamic ultrasonography. The mean interval from symptom onset to diagnosis is approximately 15.4 months, reflecting the substantial diagnostic delay associated with this condition.[34] Costal cartilage excision has been the most commonly used surgical technique, although recurrence rates of up to 17% have been reported. More recently, results from studies showed that vertical rib plating with bioabsorbable plates reduced recurrent symptoms, with recurrence rates of 3.4% compared with 17.1%, and may provide a safe alternative in both adult and pediatric populations.[35][36] Results from a pilot study demonstrated that internal subluxation of the 10th rib and the presence of a hooked rib tip may predispose individuals to the development of slipping rib syndrome.

Tumors may arise in the ribs as primary or secondary lesions. Results from a study showed a 100% cure rate after resection of benign and malignant rib tumors, with no recurrences observed.[37] Results from a review of 181 patients with malignant chest wall tumors showed that 98% underwent R0 resection, with a median of 3.5 ribs resected. Soft tissue reconstruction was performed in 40% of patients, most commonly with latissimus dorsi flaps, and rigid reconstruction was performed in 57%.[38] Chondrosarcoma is the most common primary bone malignant neoplasm of the chest wall. Among patients with primary chest wall sarcomas, R0 resection is the strongest predictor of overall survival.[39] Robot-assisted wire saw resection has emerged as a feasible surgical technique for tumors involving the first and second ribs, with no recurrences reported at 12-month follow-up in an initial series.[40]
